newsitem.title: JORDAN: Jordan says Israel housing project threatens peace.
newsitem.headline: Jordan says Israel housing project threatens peace.

text.p: Jordan said on Wednesday Israel's decision to build new Jewish housing in Arab East Jerusalem undermined the whole Arab-Israeli peace process and urged Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to reconsider.
State television said King Hussein, Israel's closest Arab ally since the two countries signed a 1994 peace treaty, sent a special envoy to warn Netanyahu of the gravity of the move.

"The decision is bound to shake the credibility of the peace process as a whole and fuel feelings of anger that will create violence and threaten the peace-building process," the television quoted the king's message as saying.

It said king Hussein urged Netanyahu to "reconsider the decision to build the settlement" of 6,500 homes for Jews at Jabal Abu Ghneim, called Har Homa by Israel, a tree-covered hill captured by Israeli forces in the 1967 Middle East war.

"Jordan considers East Jerusalem an occupied Arab territory, and any change in the status of Jerusalem unilaterally before reaching a final accord with the Palestinian Authority constitutes a real danger to peace," the king said.
"The decision will not benefit the interests of the peoples of the region, including...the Israeli people," he said.

The king, who held three hours of talks with Netanyahu on Sunday, has repeatedly warned against Israeli moves to pre-empt talks with Palestinians on the final status of self-ruled Gaza and the West Bank, including occupied East Jerusalem.
Israel says all Jerusalem is its capital. Palestinians want East Jerusalem to be capital of a future Palestinian state.

Jordanian Prime Minister Abdul-Karim al-Kabariti said Amman still wanted "to maintain the goodwill generated by achieving the Hebron deal" for limited Palestinian self-rule in the West Bank town, which Jordan helped broker last month.

"This requires dialogue...and we want to maintain good contacts with the Israeli government," he told Reuters. "But one cannot ignore the fact that this is a very grave decision, a very serious one and the repercussions could be as grave and serious."

"We feel that if the Israeli government does really go ahead, that really will threaten the whole peace process and it will poison the atmosphere necessary to continue the process in good faith," Kabariti added.
